description:
Operator-facing view of the ConfessIt observability stack: backend health, the OpenTelemetry pipeline, tracing and service graph, and logs.

Every panel is built from telemetry the stack already emits. Nothing here requires new instrumentation in the application, and the repository under observability/ is the source of truth -- this dashboard is provisioned from it, so a change to the file is a change to Grafana after a restart.

Two things worth knowing before reading a quiet panel as a fault:

* Latency panels are quantiles over request histograms. With no traffic in the window a quantile has nothing to summarise and reports no value. That is not a broken query, and it is not a zero-second response time.
* The service graph is fed by Tempo's metrics generator, which samples on its own interval. An edge can be absent for a short window after traffic stops even though the trace still exists in Tempo.

panels.description: Prometheus scrape target for the backend. Prometheus declares a target down after two failed scrapes, so this is deliberately a separate signal from the alert in the next panel.
panels.title: Backend target up

panels.description: Firing rules from observability/alerting-rules.yml, covering the backend, the collector and Tempo. The `or vector(0)` matters: when nothing fires, ALERTS has no firing series at all, and a bare sum would show "No data" exactly when the operator most wants a reassuring zero.
panels.title: Firing alerts

panels.description: Sustained request throughput as seen by the OTLP metrics pipeline.
panels.title: Request rate

panels.description: Share of requests answered 5xx, matching the expression in BackendHighErrorRate. The denominator is clamped so an idle window reads 0% rather than dividing by zero. A latency or error figure is only meaningful alongside the request-rate panel: a 0% error rate over no traffic says nothing, which is why the alert carries an explicit traffic floor.
panels.title: Error rate (5xx)

panels.description: p95 of the server request duration histogram, the same measure BackendHighLatency alerts on at 1s. No value is rendered while no request is in the window: a quantile needs samples, and reporting 0s would be a false statement rather than a quiet one.
panels.title: Latency p95

panels.description: Requests in flight right now. Sustained growth here with flat latency is the shape of a concurrency problem rather than a slow dependency.
panels.title: Active requests

panels.description: Throughput split by response status. 401 is expected volume, not an incident: the frontend probes session state, so a steady 401 line next to a flat 200 line is normal. Only 5xx is a fault, and only alongside real traffic.
panels.title: Request rate by status code

panels.description: Server-side latency distribution across the same window. The gap between p50 and p99 is the useful signal: a widening tail usually means a slow dependency on a minority of requests, while all four lines rising together means the service itself is saturated.
panels.title: Latency percentiles

panels.description: Template routes rather than raw URLs, so the path parameters of /api/profile/files/{path:path} aggregate into one bar instead of a thousand. Grouped by http_route for that reason: grouping by url would be higher cardinality and read the same.
panels.title: Top routes by rate

panels.description: Which route is slow, as opposed to how much traffic it carries. A quiet route with a high p95 is usually the interesting one, and it is invisible in a rate-ranked view.
panels.title: Top routes by latency p95

panels.description: Total requests per route over the dashboard's own range rather than a fixed five minutes, so widening the time picker answers "what actually hit this endpoint" without waiting for a rate window to fill.
panels.title: Top routes by volume

panels.description: Drill-down driven by the Route variable at the top of the dashboard. Pick one route to see its traffic and 5xx contribution against the rest of the service; leave it on All to keep the whole picture. The 5xx line disappearing entirely is the healthy state, not a missing series.
panels.title: Selected route: traffic and 5xx

panels.description: The collector's own telemetry endpoint, scraped directly by prometheus.yml rather than sent through the collector. If this is down, every panel below loses its input while the backend still looks healthy, which makes it the first place to look when this section goes blank.
panels.title: Collector up

panels.description: Spans the collector accepted and forwarded to Tempo, per second.
panels.title: Spans to Tempo /s

panels.description: Log records the collector accepted and forwarded to Loki, per second. The pipeline drops resource.service.instance.id; Loki keeps stable service identity as low-cardinality labels and high-cardinality fields as structured metadata.
panels.title: Log records to Loki /s

panels.description: Total send failures across all three signals. Spans, log records and metric points are summed because they share a unit -- items the collector could not hand off -- even though they are counted separately. A non-zero value here is the direct cause of a gap in the tracing or logs sections below.
panels.title: Export failures /s

panels.description: Accepted versus exported, per signal. The two lines of a colour should sit on top of each other: where received climbs and exported does not, data is being lost inside the collector, and the export-failures panel below names the exporter responsible.
panels.title: Telemetry throughput: received vs exported (items/s)

panels.description: Failed exports and refused items, split by exporter and receiver. A non-zero line names the hop that dropped the telemetry: otlp_grpc/tempo for traces, otlp_http/loki for logs, prometheus for metrics, and a refused count on the otlp receiver means the backend or collector rejected the payload before it was ever enqueued.
panels.title: Export failures and refusals (items/s)

panels.description: Items buffered per exporter. A queue that climbs and never drains means a downstream service is slow or unreachable, and it is visible here before any data is actually lost.
panels.title: Exporter queue size

panels.description: Collector CPU as a fraction of one core. Persistent pressure here usually shows up first as a growing export queue, since the collector is doing retry and batching work on top of forwarding.
panels.title: Collector CPU (fraction of a core)

panels.description: Collector resident set size. The collector batches in memory, so a queue that cannot drain shows up here as well as in the export-failures panels.
panels.title: Collector memory (RSS)

panels.description:
Service graph built from traces_service_graph_request_total, which the metrics generator in tempo.yml derives from the traces themselves and remote-writes into Prometheus. Reading it from Prometheus rather than through Tempo's TraceQL metrics API is deliberate: that API is not served by this Tempo build, whereas the generated series are.

The synthetic client is the external caller seen by the server span, not a deployed service, and the two database nodes are the Postgres databases the backend talks to. connection_type distinguishes those from real HTTP hops.

The queries rename their labels to id, source and target with label_replace because that is what this panel reads. Grafana's Prometheus datasource returns one frame per series with the labels attached to the value field rather than in columns of their own, so labelsToFields is what turns them into columns; naming them in the query avoids depending on a second transformation to rename them afterwards.
panels.title: Service graph (Tempo metrics generator)

panels.description:
The same edges as the graph above, as numbers, so an operator can read off which hop carries the traffic and what kind of hop it is. The graph is a shape; this is the evidence behind it.

The query renames client, server and connection_type to caller, callee and link, and clears the originals, so the table reads as three meaningful columns instead of six with each one duplicated. The value column is named through labelsToFields rather than by a second rename step.
panels.title: Service graph edges

panels.description: Slowest span operations by p95, from Tempo's span metrics. These are the spans themselves rather than the HTTP routes above, so client spans name the database statement or downstream call that a slow route is actually waiting on.
panels.title: Top spans by latency p95

panels.description: Span throughput by kind, which shows at a glance whether a change in latency came from more server work or more downstream calls.
panels.title: Span rate by kind (spans/s)

panels.description: Spans whose status is error, by name. The backend marks a request's server span as an error on an unhandled exception, so a rising line here is a real fault rather than a slow path; correlate the name with the logs panel below to find the message.
panels.title: Error-status spans by name (spans/s)

panels.description: Newest traces for the backend service, straight from Tempo's search API, so one can open a trace as a waterfall.
panels.title: Recent traces

panels.description: Log volume by the level the backend sets, using the level label the collector keeps. Counts lines per aggregation window rather than a rate, so a burst is readable as a burst.
panels.title: Log volume by level

panels.description: Which part of the code is producing the logs, read from the code.function.name field the OTLP body carries. Loki flattens the nested JSON key to attributes_code_function_name, which is why the label looks like that. An unexpected entry here is usually a chatty retry or a debug log left at INFO.
panels.title: Log volume by function

panels.description: Warnings and errors only, the series to watch when something is off. Kept separate from the level breakdown so a single red spike is not buried under INFO volume.
panels.title: Warnings and errors

panels.description: The matching log lines, newest first. Loki stores the active trace ID as structured metadata, and the TraceID derived field configured on the Loki datasource links it to the trace. The reverse direction is available from the Recent traces panel above.
panels.title: Recent warnings and errors

title: ConfessIt — Service Observability
